summary: Reports on how fast the MD5 message digest algorithm can be implemented in software and hardware, and asks whether it can keep up with the IP bandwidth available at the time. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A speed test of a fingerprint-making machine to see whether it can keep up with a fast stream of packages.

questions: can md5 keep up with network bandwidth
subtitle: Measuring how fast MD5 can authenticate data in hardware and software.

tldr.problem: IPv6 proposed MD5 as a default authentication mechanism, but the RFC needed to determine whether MD5 could run fast enough to protect data at network speeds.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC measures MD5 performance on multiple platforms in both software and hardware, analyzes the algorithm's structure to find parallelization limits, and proposes a modified version.
tldr.outcome: MD5 in software reaches only 31 to 87 Mbps depending on the platform, and hardware implementations max out at 256 Mbps. Both fall short of contemporary network speeds (100 to 622 Mbps), suggesting MD5 is unsuitable without modification or replacement.

today: RFC 1810 is informational and reflects 1995 analysis. While MD5 has since been deprecated for cryptographic purposes due to collision vulnerabilities, this RFC's performance analysis remains historically significant. Modern protocols use faster algorithms like SHA-256, and IPv6 adopted alternative authentication mechanisms.

sections.title: Why Speed Matters
sections.content:
The RFC addresses a critical question: can MD5, a cryptographic hash function proposed for IPv6 authentication, authenticate data fast enough to not become a bottleneck?

MD5 was chosen as a default optional authentication mechanism for IPv6, which should not compromise performance compared to IPv4. When enabled, MD5 must hash the entire packet including the header (with volatile fields zeroed). For authentication to be practical at network speeds, it must process data at least as fast as the network delivers it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a security check on incoming packets takes longer than the packets arrive, the router gets backed up and can't keep up with the data.

sections.title: Measured Performance
sections.content:
The RFC measures MD5 performance on eight different platforms using an optimized version of the MD5 reference implementation. On a DEC Alpha at 190 MHz, MD5 achieves 87 Mbps. Other results include 57 Mbps on a Sun SPARC-20/71, 52 Mbps on an SGI, 48 Mbps on an IBM RS/6000, 44 Mbps on an Intel Pentium, 37 Mbps on a Sun SPARC-10, 33 Mbps on an HP 9000/720, and 31 Mbps on an Intel i486.

These rates do not keep up with contemporary network technologies. For example, TCP over Fast Ethernet achieves 100 Mbps, and UDP over ATM reaches 130 Mbps. The best software implementation (87 Mbps on the DEC Alpha) falls far short of these network speeds.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing shows MD5 on the fastest computers of the time runs at 31 to 87 million bits per second, but networks are already at 100 to 130 million bits per second.

sections.title: Why MD5 Is Slow
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes the MD5 algorithm to understand its performance bottleneck. MD5 uses block chaining: each block's hash depends on the result of the previous block. This sequential dependency prevents arbitrary parallelism—blocks cannot be hashed in parallel.

Each 64-byte block is processed through 64 steps using a 4-word intermediate hash. The algorithm forms a chain where later operations depend on earlier results. A binary operation tree analysis shows the algorithm requires five time units per step and permits only 3-way parallelism at best. In software, this translates to 20 instructions per word of input. The RFC calculates that a 100 MIPS machine can support 160 Mbps (1.6 times its MIPS rate), assuming perfect parallelization.

Hardware can potentially achieve three time units per step, enabling 256 Mbps in CMOS technology. However, this still falls short of ATM link speeds exceeding 622 Mbps.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 works step-by-step in a chain where each step must wait for the previous one to finish, so it cannot be sped up much by clever tricks.

sections.title: Proposed Modifications
sections.content:
The RFC proposes modifying MD5 to support block-parallel chaining. Instead of processing all blocks in a single chain, a predetermined number of independent chains can process blocks in parallel.

For example, a 4-way or 16-way parallel chaining scheme would allow multiple blocks to be hashed simultaneously from independent seeds. The resulting digests themselves form a message that can be MD5-encoded using a single-block algorithm. A 16-way parallel chaining would support 1 Gbps data rates in CMOS hardware at current processing speeds.

The RFC notes that parallel chaining was proposed independently by the author and by Burt Kaliski of RSA. The modification aims to provide adequate bandwidth for high-speed networks without compromising security, though further analysis would be required to ensure the modified algorithm maintains adequate security properties.
sections.plainLanguage: By splitting the work into 16 independent chains instead of one, MD5 could do 16 times as much work in parallel and reach 1 billion bits per second.
